Issued at 140 AM CDT Sat Sep 5 2026

As an upper-level shortwave has moved over SD last night into this 
morning, scattered showers and storms continue to pop up and move 
over areas east of the Missouri River. The low level jet has set up 
over the area and has been helping to develop and support these 
showers and storms and it will continue to support them into the 
morning. Confidence in the timing of showers and storms is a bit low 
this morning, as the high-res models have had a harder time 
correctly showing what is actually happening when they initialize, 
which makes a person have a harder time trusting what the models 
have happening later on in the run. With warm, moist air continuing 
to move into central and northeastern SD, the environment is primed 
for showers and storms to continue to develop early this morning. 
CAPE values this morning are between 1000-2000 J/kg over central and 
northeastern SD. There are mid-level lapse rates of 7-8 C/km and 
about 30-40 kts of shear in the environment. While so far the 
scattered pulsy showers and storms haven't become severe, if they 
are able to get strong enough to tap into the environment and the 
support of the low level jet, then they could become severe. If that 
happens, then the storms could have hail up around 1 inch in 
diameter and wind gusts of 60 mph. After the low level jet dies back 
this morning, the showers and storms will likely back off for a few 
hours. 

More warm, moist air will be pushing into central and northeastern 
SD today. Temperatures will be getting up into the low 80s over far 
northeastern SD and increase to the west with highs in the upper 
90s. The higher humidity values will cause the heat index values 
over central SD to increase and get into the triple digits in some 
areas. After the showers and storms move through this morning, the 
heat and humidity will help to increase CAPE values back up to 1000-
3000 J/kg this afternoon and tonight. 850mb temperatures will also 
be warmer today, with models showing temperatures between 20-28 
degrees C. These temperatures will help to place a pretty decent cap 
over central and northeastern SD. This will likely be a similar 
situation to yesterday, where there will be scattered junky and 
pulsy showers and storms that start to pop up in the afternoon along 
the surface trough in the Rockies and the attached frontal boundary 
that stretches from northwestern to southeastern SD and showers and 
storms will continue this pattern through the night. However, with 
the potential for an upper-level shortwave to provide support to the 
storms at some point as well as an environment conducive to severe 
storms if they can break through the cap, some storms could become 
severe. Lapse rates late this afternoon into tonight will be between 
7-8 C/km and bulk shear will be between 35-45 kts. With this 
environment in place, there is a Marginal risk (level 1 of 5) for 
storms to become severe, with hail up around 1 inch and wind gusts 
of 60 mph possible. Confidence in timing for these storms is low due 
to the cap that will be in place and not knowing where and when 
something might be able to break through a weak point. 

While moisture will continue to move in over central and 
northeastern SD Sunday and Monday, the surface temperatures will 
cool slightly. High temperatures these days will be in the low 80s 
to low 90s. Instability will start to increase again over central SD 
Sunday, with CAPE values in the afternoon into the nighttime hours 
between 1000-2000 J/kg. As more upper-level shortwaves move over SD, 
they will be able to provide support for showers and storms to 
continue to develop along the surface trough and frontal boundary 
that have parked themselves over the state. Slightly cooler 
temperatures aloft will help to weaken the cap slightly, however 
with 850 temperatures still looking to be between 18-24 degrees C, 
there will still be a cap to limit storm development. As with 
yesterday and today, there could be junky, pulsy scattered showers 
and storms through the afternoon and night in this environment. 
Lapse rates look to be slightly weaker Sunday, between 6-7 C/km, as 
well as a bit weaker shear over the area compared to today. If a 
storm is able to break through the cap, there is a marginal chance 
(level 1 of 5) it could become severe Sunday afternoon through the 
overnight. The primary hazards will be hail up to 1 inch and wind 
gusts of 60 mph. While the start of Monday looks to have similar 
conditions, an upper-level trough will be pushing the ridge that 
sits over the area out, while also providing support for a cold 
front to push through overnight Monday into Tuesday. This will have 
more storms along it, but once the front pushes out of central and 
northeastern SD, we will finally get a little break from the pattern 
we have been stuck in as well as some cooler temperatures.
